title: The best day to buy and sell
objectives: Find the maximum profit from one trade in a single pass.

screens.title: One trade
screens.prose: Ten daily closes for one share, from day 0 to day 9. You may buy once and sell once, and you must buy first. Find the trade that makes the most per share.

state.caption: Tap a buy day, then a sell day

screens.question: Tap the buy day and the sell day of the best trade.

hints.text: The highest price comes early. Can you buy before it?
Look at the dip to £98 on day 3 and the rise after it.
Buy at £98 on day 3, sell at £107 on day 5: £9.

feedback.correct: Buy at £98 on day 3, sell at £107 on day 5: £9 a share.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check that the buy comes first, then compare profits.

byKey.maxmin: You picked the highest price, £110 on day 1, and the lowest, £95 on day 6. The low comes after the high, so that sells before it buys.
byKey.low: Buying at the lowest price, £95, makes £8 at most, selling at £103. Buying at £98 makes £9.
byKey.early: £102 to £110 makes £8. A later trade makes £9.

explain.text: The best trade buys at £98 on day 3 and sells at £107 on day 5, for £9. Neither day is the series' low (£95) or high (£110). The low comes after the high, so max minus min is no trade at all.

screens.title: Every pair
screens.prose: The obvious method tries every buy day with every later sell day and keeps the best profit.
screens.question: How many buy and sell pairs does it check for 10 days?

hints.text: A buy on day 0 has 9 possible sell days. A buy on day 8 has 1.
Add $9 + 8 + \dots + 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each sell day must come after its buy day.

byKey.both: You counted each pair both ways round. Selling before buying is not allowed.
byKey.all: That is every ordered pair, including a day with itself.
byKey.same: You included buying and selling on the same day, which earns nothing.

explain.text: There are $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ pairs, so the method is $O(n^2)$. Ten years of daily closes, about 2,520 days, is over 3 million pairs. One pass can do it in 2,520 steps.

screens.title: One pass
screens.prose: Walk the days once. Keep the **lowest price so far** and the **best profit so far**. Selling today earns today's price minus the lowest so far.
screens.question: Fill in the missing cells, in pounds.

hints.text: On each day, first ask whether selling today beats the best so far, then whether today is a new low.
Day 3 is a new low, £98. Day 5 sells at $107 - 98 = 9$.

feedback.correct: The lowest drops to £98 on day 3 and £95 on day 6. The best rises to £9 on day 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The best profit only changes when today's price minus the lowest beats it.

explain.text: Day 6's new low of £95 never beats £9: the best sale after it is £103. Two numbers carried through one pass replace 45 pairs. That is $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space.

screens.title: Max minus min
screens.question: What does it return, and is that a trade you could make?

options.text: 15, but no: the £110 high comes before the £95 low

options.why: You found the best trade yourself. This code ignores the order of days and returns $110 - 95 = 15$.
That needs the sale after the purchase. £110 is on day 1 and £95 on day 6, so it sells before it buys.
`max(prices) - min(prices)` is never negative. Order does not enter it at all.

hints.text: Which day holds the max, and which the min?
The max is on day 1, the min on day 6.
The code returns 15, but buying on day 6 and selling on day 1 is not a trade.

feedback.correct: 15 is the range of the prices, not a trade.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check where the max and the min sit in time.

byKey.yes: You read 15 as a trade. It sells at £110 on day 1, before buying at £95 on day 6.
byKey.nine: You expected the code to find the best trade. It returns 15, because it ignores which day comes first.

explain.text: `max - min` is the price range, and it ignores time. It equals the best trade only when the low comes before the high. Here the true answer is £9.

screens.title: When prices only fall
screens.prose:
When prices only fall, every trade loses. Our convention: do not trade, profit 0. A colleague starts from the first trade instead:

```python
low, best = prices[0], prices[1] - prices[0]
for p in prices[1:]:
    best = max(best, p - low)
    low = min(low, p)
```
screens.question: What is `best` after the loop on these four closes?

options.why: 0 is our convention, but this code never compares with 0. It starts at −6 and keeps the smallest loss.
That is last minus first. The loop keeps the best single trade, not the whole move.

hints.text: Start at $104 - 110 = -6$, then try each day.
−6, then −3, then $97 - 101 = -4$ does not beat −3.

feedback.correct: It reports a loss of £3 as the best trade.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow `best` from −6 through each day.

byKey.zero: You expected the convention. This code starts `best` at −6, so a falling series returns the smallest loss, −3.

explain.text: Starting `best` at 0 means "no trade", so a falling series returns 0. Starting from the first pair forces a trade and reports −3. Edge cases with one price, or all prices equal, also give 0 when `best` starts at 0.

screens.title: The mirror: drawdown
screens.prose: Reflect the loop: keep the **highest** price so far, and the worst fall from it. That is the maximum drawdown, measured here in pounds. It is usually quoted as a fraction of the peak, as in Python Foundations and the pytest course.
screens.question: What is this series' maximum drawdown, in pounds?

widget.accept: £15: from £110 on day 1 to £95 on day 6.
widget.label: Maximum drawdown

hints.text: Track the highest price so far, and today's fall below it.
The peak is £110 on day 1. It is never beaten.
The lowest price after the peak is £95: $110 - 95 = 15$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Measure each day's fall below the highest price so far.

byKey.first: You stopped at day 3's £98. The price falls further, to £95 on day 6.
byKey.last: That is £110 to the last close, £97. Day 6 is lower.
byKey.nine: That is the best trade. The drawdown tracks the running high, not the running low.

explain.text: The running high is £110 from day 1, and the lowest close after it is £95. Here the high comes first, so max minus min is right for the drawdown. It was wrong for the trade.

screens.title: Daily changes
screens.prose: The profit from day $i$ to day $j$ is the sum of the daily changes between them. So the best trade is the run of consecutive changes with the largest sum: the **maximum subarray**. Bar $k$ is the change into day $k$.
screens.question: Tap the run of consecutive changes with the largest sum.

hints.text: A run must be consecutive. Negative bars break it unless the gain beyond them is bigger.
Bars 4 and 5 are +3 and +6.
$3 + 6 = 9$, the same £9 as the best trade.

feedback.correct: $3 + 6 = 9$: the trade from day 3 to day 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add consecutive bars and compare the sums.

byKey.single: +8 is the biggest single change, but $3 + 6 = 9$ beats it.
byKey.late: $4 + 4 = 8$. The run into days 4 and 5 makes 9.
byKey.all-up: You picked every rise, but they are not consecutive. A trade holds through the falls in between.

explain.text: Kadane's algorithm keeps a running sum and resets it to 0 when it goes negative. That reset is the running minimum in disguise. On daily log returns, or daily P&L, the same loop finds the best stretch of a strategy.

screens.prose:
The single pass you ran, as code. Drawdown is the same loop with `max` for `min` and `high - p` for `p - low`.

```python
low, best = prices[0], 0
for p in prices[1:]:
    best = max(best, p - low)
    low = min(low, p)
```
screens.question: Why does `best` start at 0 rather than at `prices[1] - prices[0]`?

options.text: 0 is the profit of not trading, our answer when prices only fall

options.why: Both starts cost the same. The difference is the answer on a falling series.

options.text: `prices[1]` might not exist, and that is the only reason
options.why: That matters for one price, but 0 also changes the answer on a falling series: 0, not a loss.

feedback.correct: Starting at 0 means a losing trade is never reported.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What should a falling series return?

explain.text: With `best = 0`, a falling series, a single price and a flat series all return 0. The loop is $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: `best_trade(prices)` returns `(buy_index, sell_index, profit)`, buying before selling. If no trade makes money, return `(0, 0, 0)`. If trades tie, take the earliest sell day, then the earliest buy day. `prices` holds at least one price.
screens.question: Write `best_trade` in one pass.

widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests. One has 100,001 prices, so checking every pair is too slow.

hints.text: Keep the index of the lowest price so far, not just its value.
Update the best only on a strictly bigger profit, and the low only on a strictly lower price.
For each `j`: if `prices[j] - prices[lo]` beats the best, record `(lo, j, profit)`; then if `prices[j] < prices[lo]`, set `lo = j`.

feedback.correct: One pass, with the index of the running low carried along.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 only falls. Return `(0, 0, 0)`, not the smallest loss.
byKey.test-8: Test 8, `[3, 1, 4, 1, 5]`, ties: buy on day 1 or day 3. Move the low only on a strictly lower price, so day 1 stays.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 ties at 7. Update the best only on a strictly bigger profit, so the earlier sell day stays.
byKey.test-11: Test 11 has 100,001 prices. Checking every pair is about 5 billion; carry the running low instead.

explain.text: Strict comparisons give the tie rules for free: `>` keeps the earliest sell day and `<` keeps the earliest low. Starting at `(0, 0, 0)` covers one price, a flat series and a falling one.

screens.title: An upper bound for a backtest
screens.prose: A backtest on this share over the same ten days reports one long trade, in and out once. It made £12 per share. Prices are the daily closes shown.
screens.question: What do you conclude?

options.text: The backtest has a bug: no single long trade beats £9

options.why: £15 needs selling at £110 on day 1 after buying at £95 on day 6. That is selling before buying.

options.text: Plausible if it bought at the £95 low
options.why: From £95 the best sale is £103 on day 8: £8.
Profit per share does not depend on position size. The ceiling is £9 a share.

hints.text: What is the most any one buy-then-sell can make here?
You found it on the first screen.
The best trade is £9. Anything above it on these closes is impossible.

feedback.correct: £9 is a hard ceiling for one long trade on these closes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare £12 with the best possible single trade.

byKey.range: You took max minus min. The high comes first, so that is not a trade.

explain.text: `best_trade` caps any one long trade on these closes at £9, even one chosen with sight of the future. So a look-ahead bug can reach £9 but never beat it. To beat it, a backtest must sell before buying, for example through a misaligned index, or fill at other prices.

ideas: Carry two numbers through one pass: the lowest price so far and the best profit so far. That replaces $O(n^2)$ pairs with $O(n)$ steps.
Max minus min ignores time. It is the best trade only when the low comes before the high.
Reflect the loop and you get maximum drawdown; run it on daily changes and you get Kadane's maximum subarray.
